title: Section 122 — Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

content.overview: BNS s. 122 — Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation. BNS restatement of IPC 334 / 335. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 334 / 335. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 122 is the rule on “Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation”. The section provides that (1) Whoever voluntarily causes hurt on grave and sudden provocation, if he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause hurt to any person other than the person who gave the provocation, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 122 exists so that “Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
122. (1) Whoever voluntarily causes hurt on grave and sudden provocation, if he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause hurt to any person other than the person who gave the provocation, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both

(2) Whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt on grave and sudden provocation, if he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause grievous hurt to any person other than the person who gave the provocation, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both

learningObjectives: Master the mitigated offences of causing hurt or grievous hurt on grave and sudden provocation under BNS s. 122.
Analyze the application of Section 101 Exception 1 provisos to Section 122 under the statutory Explanation.
Contrast sub-section (1) (hurt on provocation: up to 1 month or fine up to ₹1,000) with sub-section (2) (grievous hurt on provocation: up to 5 years and fine).
Understand the consolidation of IPC ss. 334 and 335.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 122 consolidates mitigated provisions for hurt caused under provocation: sub-section (1) provides that whoever voluntarily causes hurt on grave and sudden provocation, if he neither intends nor knows himself likely to cause hurt to any other person, shall be punished with imprisonment up to one month, or fine up to one thousand rupees, or both; sub-section (2) provides that whoever voluntarily causes grievous hurt on grave and sudden provocation shall be punished with imprisonment up to five years, or fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or both.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Recognizes human frailty by mitigating penal consequences when non-fatal physical harm is inflicted under the immediate loss of self-control caused by grave and sudden provocation.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 122 (consolidating IPC ss. 334 and 335).
Sub-section (1): Voluntarily causing hurt on grave and sudden provocation — imprisonment up to one month, or fine up to ₹1,000, or both.

Sub-section (2): Voluntarily causing grievous hurt on grave and sudden provocation — imprisonment of either description up to five years, or fine up to ₹10,000, or both (fine modernized from ₹2,000 under IPC 335).

Explanation: Explicitly incorporates the provisos to Exception 1 of Section 101: provocation must not be sought or voluntarily provoked; not given by lawful acts of public servants; and not given in exercise of private defence.
essentialIngredients: The accused caused hurt (sub-section 1) OR grievous hurt (sub-section 2) to a person.
The act was done under the immediate influence of grave and sudden provocation.
The provocation deprived the accused of self-control.
The accused neither intended nor knew himself likely to cause hurt to any person other than the provoker.
The provocation satisfies the three provisos of Section 101 Exception 1.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 122 consolidates former IPC 334 and 335. Just as grave and sudden provocation reduces murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder, it equally mitigates non-fatal hurt. The law recognizes that an individual subjected to sudden and grave indignity or provocation may temporarily lose self-control. The statutory Explanation subjects Section 122 to the exact three provisos governing Exception 1 of Section 101: (1) the provocation must not be sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender as an excuse; (2) the provocation must not be given by anything done in obedience to law by a public servant; and (3) the provocation must not be given by anything done in lawful exercise of private defence. Furthermore, the mitigation only applies if the harm was directed at the person who gave the provocation, not an innocent third party.
examples: Teaching example (Sub-section 1 - Slap on grave provocation): A person is subjected to an extreme, sudden, and obscene personal insult regarding his deceased parents by an antagonist. Deprived of self-control, he immediately slaps the antagonist. Under s. 122(1), the punishment is capped at one month imprisonment or ₹1,000 fine.

Teaching example (Sub-section 2 - Grievous hurt on provocation): A shopkeeper discovers an intruder actively molesting his daughter in the shop backroom; enraged by this grave and sudden provocation, he strikes the intruder with a wooden plank, fracturing the intruder's collarbone. The offence is mitigated to s. 122(2) (up to five years and fine).
distinctions: Section 122(1) vs Section 115: Section 115 carries up to 1 year for unprovoked hurt; Section 122(1) mitigates the sentence to 1 month where grave and sudden provocation is established.
Section 122(2) vs Section 117(2): Section 117(2) carries up to 7 years for unprovoked grievous hurt; Section 122(2) mitigates the maximum to 5 years.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who fractured the wrist of an individual who suddenly slapped him without warning can claim the benefit of s. 122(2).
Rule: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt under the immediate influence of grave and sudden provocation reduces liability to BNS s. 122(2).
Application: The unprovoked physical assault was sudden and grave, provoking an immediate retaliatory blow without cooling time.
Conclusion: The accused is entitled to mitigation under BNS s. 122(2).
